transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well... I’m here because I just feel like I don’t deserve the trust people put in me. I keep replaying these small clinical imperfections in my head, over and over, as if they prove I’m a dangerous doctor. Like, I'll be sitting in my office—which, by the way, has this really terrible fluorescent lighting. It hums. Have you ever noticed how some bulbs just hum constantly? I tried telling the building manager, Dave, about it last Tuesday. Dave is always wearing these bright yellow ties, which is a choice, I guess. He told me he'd fix it, but he never did. I ended up trying to buy a desk lamp at Target to use instead, but the line was so long I just left my cart right in the aisle. I felt a little bad about leaving the cart, honestly. But anyway... yeah. I just keep thinking about my minor mistakes with patients and how I'm probably a danger to them.
Do you feel like you're unable to control these thoughts about your clinical imperfections?

I mean... I don't really know if I can control them or not. I try to distract myself when they happen. Like, the other night I tried reading this book to get my mind off work. It was about the history of the stethoscope. Did you know Rene Laennec invented it because he felt awkward putting his ear directly on a female patient's chest? He just rolled up a piece of paper. Paper back then was so much thicker, you know, almost like parchment. I was actually looking at some vintage stationery online recently, thinking maybe I should start writing actual letters instead of emails. It feels more personal. But the shipping costs are just ridiculous. They wanted twenty-five dollars just to ship a single notebook from London. I just couldn't justify spending that on a notebook, especially with the exchange rate being what it is right now. But... wait, what were we talking about? Controlling the thoughts? Yeah, I'm not really sure.
Do you feel like you have to do certain things in a specific way or repeat certain actions to feel okay?

No, not really. I don't have rituals or anything like that. I mean, I do have a specific way I like my coffee in the morning, but that's just a preference. I go to this little place down the street from my apartment—well, it used to be a dry cleaner, actually. You can still sort of smell the chemicals if you go in right when they open. The barista there, her name is Chloe, she has this tattoo of a very anatomically correct heart on her forearm. It's actually really well done, the shading on the ventricles is impressive. I asked her about it once and she said she got it in Portland. I've never been to Portland. I hear it rains a lot, which I don't think I'd mind. Rain is kind of soothing, isn't it? Except when it ruins your shoes. I bought these Italian leather loafers last month and they got completely soaked on the walk from my car to the hospital. But no, I don't feel like I *have* to do things a certain way to feel okay. Just the thoughts, mostly.
Do you think these thoughts about your clinical imperfections are unreasonable or excessive?

Well, I mean... I don't know if they're unreasonable. They feel very real to me, you know? Like they're completely justified because I'm a doctor and people's lives are in my hands. Hands are actually so incredibly complex, anatomically speaking. There are 27 bones in the human hand. I remember studying them in med school, trying to memorize all the carpals. Scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum... I used to use this mnemonic device about a boat, I think? Or maybe it was about a moon. My anatomy professor, Dr. Henderson, he had these massive hands. Like, huge. He could probably palm a watermelon if he wanted to. He also had this really thick Scottish accent, which made lectures kind of difficult to follow sometimes. He'd always talk about going back to Edinburgh for the summer. I've always wanted to visit Scotland. The Highlands look so beautiful in pictures, all that green and the mist. I bet the air smells amazing there, not like the city air here. It's always so smoggy, especially in August. But yeah... I don't know if the thoughts are excessive. They just are what they are.
Are these thoughts about your clinical imperfections affecting your ability to function at work or in your daily activities?

Well, I'm still showing up to the clinic every day. My office is right next to the breakroom, and they actually just installed this new espresso machine in there. It's a La Marzocco, I think. Really beautiful stainless steel, but it is incredibly loud. Whenever someone steams milk, it sounds exactly like a jet engine taking off. I don't even drink espresso that late in the day anymore because it just completely ruins my sleep. Sleep hygiene is so crucial, you know? I was reading about William Halsted recently, the surgeon who basically created the modern residency training system at Johns Hopkins. He was famously addicted to cocaine, which is how he managed to stay awake and operate for days on end. It’s wild to think cocaine used to be completely legal and in everything, even Coca-Cola. Imagine trying to prescribe something like that today, the pharmacy would lose their minds. 

But, um, what was I saying? Oh, right, functioning at work. Yeah, I'm still going in, but I've had to ask for help with a lot of the non-urgent administrative work. I just can't seem to get through the paperwork. And outside of the clinic, I've mostly been avoiding social plans entirely. I just don't really trust my own judgment right now, and I definitely don't have the energy for people. It’s like a battery that just won't hold a charge anymore. My phone has actually been doing that lately, dying when it says it still has forty percent left. I probably need to take it to the Apple store, but the one at the mall is always so crowded. But yeah, I guess the thoughts have started to affect how reliably I function at work, and how connected I am outside of it.
Do you feel anxious when you're not thinking about these clinical imperfections?

Anxious? Um, no, I wouldn't say that. When I'm actually able to stop thinking about my clinical decisions, I don't really feel anxious. I mostly just feel... empty, I guess? Or just incredibly tired. I actually fell asleep on my couch yesterday afternoon watching this documentary about the Mariana Trench. Have you ever looked into deep-sea gigantism? It's fascinating how creatures down there grow so massive just because of the pressure and the cold. They showed this colossal squid that was, like, forty feet long. I can't even imagine being in one of those tiny submersibles, thousands of feet underwater in total darkness. The pressure per square inch is astronomical. They have to make the viewports out of this specialized acrylic because regular glass would just shatter instantly under that kind of weight. 

I actually had a glass coffee table once that shattered completely out of nowhere. Tempered glass. The manufacturer said it was spontaneous breakage from some microscopic flaw during the cooling process. It sounded like a gunshot in my living room. It took me weeks to vacuum all the little glass cubes out of my rug. It was this really nice Persian rug, too, hand-woven. The red and gold in it really warmed up the room. I ended up just rolling it up and putting it in the closet because I was so paranoid about stepping on a stray piece of glass barefoot. 

But, um... wait, what was the question? Oh, anxiety. Right. No, I don't think I get anxious when my mind is off the clinic. If anything, it's a relief, but mostly I just don't feel much of anything at all.
Do these thoughts about your clinical imperfections come into your mind against your will?

Against my will? Um... I don't think so. It's not like they're forced into my head or anything. They're just my normal thoughts, they just happen. It's not like a pop-up ad on a computer, you know? 

Speaking of which, my laptop has been getting so many of those lately. I think I accidentally clicked on something weird when I was trying to download a PDF of a journal article last week. Now it just randomly opens tabs for, like, discount auto insurance and weird dietary supplements. I've tried running a virus scan, but it takes forever. The progress bar always gets to ninety-nine percent and then just hangs there for an hour. It's incredibly frustrating. I used to be pretty good with computers, actually. I built my own desktop back in undergrad. I bought all the parts online—the motherboard, the GPU, the power supply. Getting the thermal paste exactly right on the processor is actually pretty stressful. If you use too much, it spills over and ruins the pins. If you use too little, it overheats. It's a very delicate balance. 

Kind of like baking, I guess. I tried making sourdough a couple of years ago like everyone else did, but my starter just ended up smelling exactly like nail polish remover. I read that means it's hungry and producing too much acetic acid, but it just grossed me out too much. I ended up throwing the whole mason jar away in the outside trash because I couldn't get the smell out of the glass and I didn't want it in my kitchen. The raccoons probably got to it. We have these massive raccoons in my neighborhood. They figure out how to open the bungee cords on the bins... 

But, uh... sorry. What were we talking about? Oh, the thoughts. Yeah, no, they don't feel like they're against my will. I'm just thinking them.
Do you feel like these thoughts about clinical imperfections are intrusive, meaning they interrupt your other thoughts?

Intrusive? Um... no, not really. They don't interrupt anything. It's more like they're just... always there, running in the background. Like a radio left on in another room. 

My grandfather used to do that. He had this old wooden Zenith radio in his garage, and he'd just leave it tuned to AM talk radio all day and night. He said it kept the mice away. I'm not sure if that actually works, scientifically speaking, but his garage was always spotless. He was a mechanic, mostly worked on old Fords. He had this beautiful 1965 Mustang, cherry red, that he was restoring. The smell of oil and gasoline in that garage was so strong, it would cling to your clothes for hours. I used to sit on a milk crate and watch him rebuild carburetors. It's a dying art, really, everything is fuel-injected and computerized now. You can't even change your own oil on some of these new European cars without a special tool that costs hundreds of dollars. It's a total racket. 

I bought a German car once, right after I finished medical school. I thought it was this great reward to myself, but the maintenance was an absolute nightmare. The check engine light came on after three months, and it turned out some sensor had failed. Just a tiny piece of plastic and wire, but it cost a fortune to replace because they had to take half the engine block apart to get to it. I ended up trading it in for a Honda two years later. Best decision I ever made. The Honda is so reliable, it's almost boring. But I guess boring is good when you just need to get to work. 

But, um... wait. Interrupting thoughts? Right. No, they don't interrupt. They're just kind of... always playing.
Do you find these thoughts about your clinical imperfections to be distressing?

Distressing? Um... no, I don't think so. It's more like they're just facts. I don't get worked up or stressed out about them. 

Speaking of stress, the one thing that really used to cause me distress was the sound of the emergency pager when I was doing my residency. It had this incredibly piercing, high-pitched beep that would just cut through anything. I swear I still hear it sometimes when I'm falling asleep. It's amazing that hospitals still rely on pagers, honestly. The technology is so outdated. We still use fax machines, too. It's the twenty-first century, and we're sending sensitive medical records over phone lines that make that awful screeching noise. 

My family actually got our first computer in, like, 1999, and I remember tying up the phone line for hours just to use dial-up internet. My mom was always yelling at me because she was waiting for a call from my aunt in Florida. My aunt lived in this retirement community near Tampa, and they had golf carts everywhere. Everyone just drove these little electric golf carts to the grocery store. It seemed so dangerous to me, mixing golf carts with regular traffic, but they had special lanes for them. I tried driving one once when we visited, but the steering was so loose I almost drove it into a water hazard on the golf course. They had all these warning signs about alligators in the ponds. It's crazy to think people just live right next to prehistoric predators like that and think nothing of it. 

But... sorry, I lost my train of thought again. Did you ask if I was upset? Yeah, no. The thoughts aren't distressing. They're just there.
Do you ever find yourself trying to ignore or suppress these thoughts about your clinical imperfections?

Ignore them? Um... no, not really. I don't try to push them away or anything. Like I said, they're just facts, so there's no real point in trying to suppress them. 

Trying to ignore things usually just makes it worse anyway. Like a few months ago, I tried to ignore this water stain on the ceiling of my apartment. I just kept telling myself it was an old stain, but then the paint started bubbling. My landlord is this guy who insists on doing all the maintenance himself to save money, so he came over with this cheap sealant that smelled strongly of vinegar. Reminds me of that sourdough starter I was talking about earlier. But he just patched over the ceiling, and of course, a week later the pipe completely gave out while I was at the clinic. It ruined my living room rug. It was this beautiful Persian rug I found at an estate sale. 

Have you ever been to an estate sale? They're fascinating, honestly. You just walk through someone's entire life laid out on folding tables with little neon price tags. I bought this antique brass globe at that same sale, but the geography is all outdated. It's from the 1920s, so it has places like Siam and the Belgian Congo. It's really interesting to see how the borders have shifted over a century. Mapmaking used to be such an art form before satellite imaging. Now we just have Google Earth and you can zoom in on someone's backyard from space. It's a little creepy when you think about it, the total lack of privacy we have now. 

But, um... sorry, I'm rambling again. Did you ask if I try to ignore the thoughts? Yeah, no, I don't. I just let them be.
Do you feel like these thoughts about your clinical imperfections are repetitive?

Repetitive? Yeah, I guess they are. I mean, that's kind of why I'm here. I just keep replaying these small clinical imperfections over and over in my head, like they prove I'm some sort of dangerous doctor. I just feel like I don't deserve the trust people put in me. 

Trust is a weird thing, though, isn't it? Like, we trust people every day without even thinking about it. You trust the barista to not poison your coffee. You trust the guy driving the bus to not drive it off a bridge. I used to take the bus a lot when I was in undergrad. It was this old city bus that always smelled like wet wool and ozone. The driver was this guy named Stan who always wore these mirrored aviator sunglasses, even when it was raining. He had this little bobblehead hula girl on the dashboard that would just shake wildly every time we hit a pothole. 

The potholes in that city were legendary. I lost a hubcap to one once. Just flew right off my car and rolled down a storm drain. It's funny how infrastructure just crumbles if you don't constantly maintain it. Kind of like teeth. If you don't floss, it all goes to hell. I had this dentist when I was a kid who would give out these little plastic spider rings instead of stickers. I always thought that was a weird choice for a medical professional. Spiders don't exactly scream "hygiene." 

But... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right. Replaying the thoughts. Yeah, they just keep looping. Like I'm just a fraud waiting to be found out.
Are these repetitive thoughts about clinical imperfections making it harder for you to concentrate on your daily tasks?

Yeah, it really is. I mean, I’ll read the same lab result or inbox message, like, five times and still feel completely unsure of what I just read. It makes even simple admin decisions take an embarrassing amount of time. 

Speaking of admin, our clinic just updated the messaging system on our Electronic Health Records, and the new interface is just... it's atrocious. The color scheme is this blinding neon blue. Who picks neon blue for something you have to stare at for twelve hours a day? It completely strains your eyes. It reminds me of this laser tag arena I used to go to for birthday parties when I was a kid. They had all these blacklights everywhere, and if you wore a white shirt, you'd just glow like a beacon and everyone would target you. I always wore this dark green sweater, even in the middle of summer, just to blend into the walls. 

It was always so hot in there, though, because you're just running around in the dark. They sold these giant slushies at the concession stand to cool you down, the kind that turn your tongue bright blue for a week. I think the flavor was supposed to be "blue raspberry," which isn't even a real fruit, you know? Have you ever seen a blue raspberry in nature? It's just a marketing gimmick they made up in the seventies because they had too many red flavors, like cherry and strawberry, and they needed a way to tell the popsicles apart. It's funny how things like that just become accepted as normal. 

But, um... wait, what was the question? Oh, concentrating. Right. Yeah, it's just really hard to focus right now. I just stare at my inbox and nothing really registers.
Do you feel like these thoughts about your clinical imperfections are in line with your own beliefs and values about yourself as a doctor?

Um... I don't know. I guess so? I mean, I've always held myself to a pretty high standard, so maybe they are in line with that. But I'm not really sure what my values are anymore, honestly. 

Values are strange, aren't they? Like, they change so much depending on where you are in life. When I was in medical school, my biggest value was just surviving on four hours of sleep and vending machine coffee. There was this one machine in the basement of the library that had these stale cheese crackers. They were always slightly crushed, but they were the only thing that kept me awake during anatomy lectures. The anatomy lab always smelled like formaldehyde, which is a smell you never really get out of your nose. It just lingers. 

It kind of smells like this weird antique store my grandmother used to take me to when I was little. She loved collecting these porcelain dolls with the creepy glass eyes that always felt like they were watching you. She had an entire cabinet of them in her guest room. I hated sleeping in there. I always made sure to throw a blanket over the glass doors so they couldn't see me. 

But... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, my values as a doctor. Yeah, I don't know. I just... I don't really know if these thoughts match up with anything right now.
Do you feel like these thoughts about your clinical imperfections are a part of who you are, or do they feel alien to you?

I mean, they definitely feel like a part of who I am now. Like I was saying earlier, I'm here because I really feel like I don't deserve the trust people put in me. I just keep replaying those small clinical imperfections over and over, like they're absolute proof that I'm a dangerous doctor. 

It's exhausting, honestly. Being dangerous, I mean. Well, not that I'm actually out there hurting people on purpose, but you know what I mean. It makes me think of those warning labels on things. Like, "Danger: High Voltage." I saw one of those signs on a transformer box when I was walking through the park last week. The park has this really nice duck pond, but there are all these signs telling you not to feed the ducks bread. Apparently, it's really bad for them. It gives them this condition called "angel wing" where their wings grow all weird and they can't fly. 

It's sad, really, because people just want to do something nice and feed the ducks, but they end up hurting them without even realizing it. Kind of like how people give kids too much sugar. My cousin has a five-year-old, and he just feeds him juice boxes all day. Those things are basically just liquid candy. I tried to tell him once, but he just brushed it off. He's always been stubborn, though. Even when we were kids, if we were playing Monopoly, he would absolutely refuse to trade properties, even if it meant he was going to lose. He just had to hoard all the railroads. 

But... sorry, what was the question? Oh, if the thoughts feel alien. No, they don't feel alien. They just feel like the truth about me right now. Like I'm just a hazard to my patients.
Do you feel like these thoughts about your clinical imperfections are causing you a lot of emotional pain?

Emotional pain? Um... I don't really know if I'd call it pain. I'm not sure. Pain is such a subjective thing to measure, anyway. Like that 1 to 10 scale we use in the clinic, the Wong-Baker FACES chart? I've always hated that chart. The face for a number 8 doesn't even look like it's hurting, it just looks furious. It looks exactly like my old high school gym teacher, Mr. Henderson, whenever someone forgot their gym clothes. He'd make you sit on these cold metal bleachers for the entire period. 

Those bleachers were brutal in the winter. They'd just suck all the body heat right out of you. My friend Mark actually got his tongue stuck to a metal pole near those bleachers on a dare once. It was exactly like that scene in A Christmas Story. The school nurse had to come out with a thermos of warm water to unstick him. Mark was always doing stuff like that for attention, though. He once ate an entire jar of mayonnaise for ten bucks in the cafeteria. Just sat there with a spoon and ate it. It was revolting. The smell of mayo still kind of turns my stomach. Actually, the cafeteria at the hospital uses way too much mayo in their chicken salad. It's basically just a thick white paste. I really don't understand how anyone eats it. 

But... wait, what were you asking? Oh, right, emotional pain. Yeah, I don't really know. I haven't really thought of it as pain, so I'm not sure how to answer that.
Are these thoughts affecting your personal relationships or leisure activities outside of work?

Yeah, I suppose it is. I've been avoiding social plans lately because I just don't trust my judgment, or my energy for that matter. 

Judgment is a tricky thing, though. Like, my buddy Dave clearly had zero judgment when he bought this beat-up sailboat off Craigslist last summer. He didn't even know how to sail. He just thought it would be a fun weekend project. We spent three weekends sanding the hull, and that fiberglass dust gets absolutely everywhere. It is the worst itch you can imagine. I actually had to throw away my favorite pair of jeans because I couldn't wash the fiberglass out of them. They were those perfect Levi's that take like five years to break in. It's impossible to find good jeans now, you know? They all have that weird stretchy spandex stuff in them. I miss when denim was just heavy, stiff cotton. My dad used to wear these rigid denim overalls when he worked in the garden. He grew these massive heirloom tomatoes every year. The squirrels would always take one bite out of the very best ones and just leave them rotting on the vine. It used to drive him absolutely crazy. He tried putting up this fake plastic owl to scare them away, but the squirrels ended up just sitting right on the owl's head. 

But... sorry, I lost track again. You were asking about outside of work? Right. So yeah, I avoid social plans. And even though I'm still showing up to the clinic, it's definitely starting to affect how reliably I function there. I've had to ask for help with a lot of the non-urgent administrative work because I just can't get through it. It's really affecting my reliability at the office and how connected I feel outside of it.
Do you feel like these thoughts about your clinical imperfections are consistent with your self-image as a competent doctor?

Competent? I mean... I used to think I was. Back in residency, I actually felt pretty confident. I got really good at suturing because I would practice on bananas at home. Bananas are actually terrible for it, though, the peels just mush up if you pull the thread too tight. My roommate, Greg, used to just eat the bananas after I was done practicing on them. He was unbelievably cheap. He would buy these heavily dented cans of soup from this discount grocery outlet just to save thirty cents. Once he bought a can of clam chowder that was expired by like three years. Clam chowder is already a pretty risky soup, you know? It's dairy and seafood. Leaving that in a metal can for years just seems like a guaranteed recipe for botulism. Botulism is a fascinating mechanism, though, the way the toxin just completely blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction. It's wild that people actually pay to have it injected into their foreheads just to get rid of wrinkles. 

But... wait, sorry. What was the question? My self-image? Right. No, it's like I was saying earlier... I just don't feel like I deserve the trust people put in me at all. Any idea of being a "competent" doctor feels completely gone. I just keep replaying every single little clinical imperfection in my head, over and over, and to me, they just prove that I'm a dangerous doctor. So no, it doesn't fit with being competent anymore.
Are these thoughts about clinical imperfections interfering with your ability to enjoy your free time or hobbies?

Free time? Yeah... I mean, I used to do a lot with my free time. I used to plan these huge weekend hikes, get up super early for sunrise photos, and cook these massive Indonesian dinners for my friends. 

Indonesian food is so incredibly complex, you know? The prep work alone takes hours. You have to grind all the spices by hand in a mortar and pestle to really get the oils out. Lemongrass, galangal, candlenuts... candlenuts are actually slightly toxic if you eat them raw. You have to cook them first. It's funny how many things we eat that are technically poisonous in their natural state. Like kidney beans. If you don't boil kidney beans long enough, they have this protein in them that causes severe gastrointestinal distress. I actually saw a patient in the ER during med school who undercooked a slow-cooker chili and basically poisoned his entire family. Slow cookers don't always get hot enough to destroy the toxin, which is a major design flaw if you ask me. I actually ended up giving my slow cooker away to a thrift store after that. Thrift stores are fascinating, though. You can find the most bizarre things in them. I once found an entire taxidermy squirrel wearing a tiny cowboy hat. Who even makes something like that? And more importantly, who buys it and then decides to donate it? 

But... wait, what were we talking about? Hobbies, right. Yeah, so... for months now, all those things—the hiking, the photography, the cooking—they just feel like these massive obligations. I just can't make myself care about them anymore. I don't enjoy them at all.
Do you feel like these thoughts about your clinical imperfections are in conflict with your own self-image or values as a doctor?

I feel like we might have just talked about my self-image, right? But as for my values... I don't really know. I mean, when I took the oath at graduation, I felt like I had very clear values. 

Graduation was so incredibly hot that day, though. We were all wearing those heavy robes. The academic regalia for a medical degree has those thick green velvet stripes on the sleeves. Velvet is such an impractical fabric. It crushes so easily and you can't really wash it. My aunt had this vintage crushed velvet sofa in her living room that nobody was allowed to sit on. It was this hideous mustard yellow color. She kept it covered in clear plastic most of the time, which completely defeats the purpose of having a velvet sofa, if you ask me. When you sat on the plastic in the summer, your legs would sweat and stick to it, and it made this horrible peeling sound when you tried to stand up. She had these two little pugs that would just lay on the plastic all day panting. Pugs have such terrible respiratory issues because of how they've been bred. It's actually really sad how we've prioritized aesthetic traits over basic biological function in dog breeding. They can barely breathe when it gets above seventy degrees. 

But... sorry, I'm rambling again. You were asking about my values being in conflict? I honestly don't know how to answer that differently than what I just said a minute ago. I'm just not sure what my values even look like right now, other than feeling like I'm a danger to my patients. I haven't really noticed anything beyond that.
Do you feel like these thoughts about your clinical imperfections are something that you would normally think, or are they foreign to your usual way of thinking about yourself?

Normally think? No. No, not at all. I mean, before all of this started... before this whole depressive period really kicked in after I got that clinic award, I never thought like this. 

That award ceremony was so strange, actually. They held it at this Italian restaurant downtown that had these really elaborate, fake grapevines hanging from the ceiling. Fake plants in restaurants always gather so much dust. I remember looking up during the speeches and just seeing these thick layers of grey dust on the plastic leaves right above where people were eating their pasta. Dust is mostly dead skin cells, you know, which is kind of a repulsive thought when you're trying to eat chicken parmigiana. Chicken parmigiana is such a heavy dish anyway. My grandmother used to make it, but she would always overcook the chicken until it was basically the texture of a shoe sole. She insisted that poultry had to be cooked to an absolute minimum of 185 degrees just to be safe. She had this old dial meat thermometer that I'm pretty sure was broken and permanently read about 20 degrees too low. So she was probably cooking things to over 200 degrees. It's a miracle we didn't all chip a tooth on her Sunday dinners. She also used to make this Jell-O salad with shredded carrots in it. Why did people in the 1970s think it was acceptable to put vegetables inside gelatin? It's structurally unsound and texturally horrifying. 

Wait, sorry. I'm doing it again. What were we talking about? Oh, if these thoughts are foreign to me. Yeah, completely foreign. Like I was saying, before this low, guilty state started after the award, I had never heard patient voices in my head. And I definitely had never been convinced that I had secretly harmed people, especially when there's evidence right in front of me showing I didn't. These voices and these fixed beliefs that I've ruined people's lives... they only ever show up when I'm in this awful, depressed state. It's definitely not my usual way of thinking.

I used to sit on a milk crate and watch him rebuild carburetors. It's a dying art, really, everything is fuel-injected and computerized now. You can't even change your own oil on some of these new European cars without a special tool that costs hundreds of dollars. It's a total racket. 

I bought a German car once, right after I finished medical school. I thought it was this great reward to myself, but the maintenance was an absolute nightmare. Best decision I ever made. The Honda is so reliable, it's almost boring. But I guess boring is good when you just need to get to work.

Thrift stores are fascinating, though. You can find the most bizarre things in them. I once found an entire taxidermy squirrel wearing a tiny cowboy hat. Who even makes something like that? Graduation was so incredibly hot that day, though. We were all wearing those heavy robes. The academic regalia for a medical degree has those thick green velvet stripes on the sleeves. Velvet is such an impractical fabric. It crushes so easily and you can't really wash it. My aunt had this vintage crushed velvet sofa in her living room that nobody was allowed to sit on. It was this hideous mustard yellow color. She kept it covered in clear plastic most of the time, which completely defeats the purpose of having a velvet sofa, if you ask me. When you sat on the plastic in the summer, your legs would sweat and stick to it, and it made this horrible peeling sound when you tried to stand up. She had these two little pugs that would just lay on the plastic all day panting. Pugs have such terrible respiratory issues because of how they've been bred. It's actually really sad how we've prioritized aesthetic traits over basic biological function in dog breeding. They can barely breathe when it gets above seventy degrees. 

But... sorry, I'm rambling again. You were asking about my values being in conflict? I honestly don't know how to answer that differently than what I just said a minute ago. I'm just not sure what my values even look like right now, other than feeling like I'm a danger to my patients. I haven't really noticed anything beyond that.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's thoughts are ego-dystonic
doctor.question: Do you feel like these thoughts about your clinical imperfections are something that you would normally think, or are they foreign to your usual way of thinking about yourself?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Before this depressive period after the clinic award, I had never heard patient voices or been convinced I had secretly harmed people despite evidence. The voices and fixed guilty beliefs only show up when I’m in this low, guilty state.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if these thoughts (delusions/guilt) are part of the patient's normal baseline or if they are foreign/new. This directly addresses whether these psychotic and guilty symptoms are exclusive to the current depressive episode.

patient.answer:
Normally think? No. No, not at all. I mean, before all of this started... before this whole depressive period really kicked in after I got that clinic award, I never thought like this. 

That award ceremony was so strange, actually. They held it at this Italian restaurant downtown that had these really elaborate, fake grapevines hanging from the ceiling. Fake plants in restaurants always gather so much dust. I remember looking up during the speeches and just seeing these thick layers of grey dust on the plastic leaves right above where people were eating their pasta. Dust is mostly dead skin cells, you know, which is kind of a repulsive thought when you're trying to eat chicken parmigiana. Chicken parmigiana is such a heavy dish anyway. My grandmother used to make it, but she would always overcook the chicken until it was basically the texture of a shoe sole. She insisted that poultry had to be cooked to an absolute minimum of 185 degrees just to be safe. She had this old dial meat thermometer that I'm pretty sure was broken and permanently read about 20 degrees too low. So she was probably cooking things to over 200 degrees. It's a miracle we didn't all chip a tooth on her Sunday dinners. She also used to make this Jell-O salad with shredded carrots in it. Why did people in the 1970s think it was acceptable to put vegetables inside gelatin? It's structurally unsound and texturally horrifying. 

Wait, sorry. I'm doing it again. What were we talking about? Oh, if these thoughts are foreign to me. Yeah, completely foreign. Like I was saying, before this low, guilty state started after the award, I had never heard patient voices in my head. And I definitely had never been convinced that I had secretly harmed people, especially when there's evidence right in front of me showing I didn't. These voices and these fixed beliefs that I've ruined people's lives... they only ever show up when I'm in this awful, depressed state. It's definitely not my usual way of thinking.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits symptoms of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), including intrusive thoughts about clinical imperfections, repetitive replaying of these thoughts, and significant distress and impairment in social and occupational functioning. While the patient also shows some signs of depression, such as loss of interest in hobbies and feelings of emptiness, the primary symptoms suggest OCD.
